comparison: Both address the auditory cortex control analysis (C36-C37). OpenEval finds this control adequately addresses auditory confounds through temporal dissociation. Peer reviewers find the control insufficient and request fuller presentation with figures and statistics, stating the auditory cue issue 'must be addressed' more comprehensively.

Both strongly support the effector-specific decoding findings across brain regions (C4, C5, C15, C16, C31, C32, C34). OpenEval emphasizes the statistical rigor and convergence of results. Peer reviewers explicitly endorse these as 'a really important aspect of the findings' and only request better presentation in the abstract and introduction.

Both support the occipitotemporal decoding findings (C59-C61, C66, C70). OpenEval notes the temporal specificity provides strong evidence against sensory feedback explanations. Peer reviewers explicitly endorse this interpretation, stating it 'resonates' with theories about ventral stream organization and encourage fuller theoretical discussion.

Both support the broader theoretical interpretations about OTC organization and motor-visual coupling (C69, C73, C77). OpenEval finds these appropriately qualified and reasonable. Peer reviewers explicitly encourage this framework and want it developed more fully, noting the authors 'come close to, but shy away from' fully embracing these implications.

Both address temporal decoding characteristics (C28-C30). OpenEval finds the time-resolved analyses provide strong evidence for planning-specific signals. Peer reviewers note insufficient discussion of temporal development and that temporal findings are relevant to addressing the auditory cue confound concern that 'must be addressed.'

Both address across-effector decoding (C3, C18, C19). OpenEval finds converging evidence supports these claims with appropriate statistical controls. Peer reviewers raise critical concern that auditory cues were identical across effectors and 'could be responsible for some or even all of the apparently cross-effector classification,' directly challenging the interpretation.

Both address aIPS findings and interpretations (C50-C51, plus C42, C45 in OpenEval). OpenEval supports the distinction between recruitment versus shared representations. Peer reviewers find the pattern 'somewhat surprising' and request reconciliation of how regions showing across-effector decoding also show better hand than tool decoding.

Both address voxel weight analysis (C35). OpenEval finds the lack of spatial structure reasonable given low decoding accuracies and trial variability. Peer reviewers request more detailed presentation of voxel weights to help reconcile different decoding effects across regions.

Both address motor cortex control findings (C39-C40). OpenEval finds these provide important validation of the MVPA approach with expected effector-specific coding. Peer reviewers find it surprising that regions showing across-effector decoding also show effector-specific effects and request reconciliation.

Both address the overall hierarchical framework and main findings (C2, C6). OpenEval supports the hierarchical interpretation following logically from spatial distribution of representations. Peer reviewers provide general endorsement, with the reviewing editor calling it 'excellent work' with a 'well-thought-out and sophisticated approach.'

Both address forward-state estimation interpretation (C67). OpenEval notes this is appropriately framed as speculative possibility rather than definitive conclusion. Peer reviewers support the theoretical framework linking motor planning to visual organization and encourage fuller development of these ideas.

OpenEval addresses speculation about object feature coding mechanisms (C53-C54), noting this is explicitly presented as speculation without direct testing. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific mechanistic claims.

OpenEval addresses extensive literature citations and theoretical context (C1, C7-C14, C25-C27, C41, C43-C44, C48-C49, C52, C55-C58, C68, C71-C72, C74-C76). These represent established knowledge appropriately cited. No specific peer review evaluation of these background claims found, though peer R9 addresses some overlapping theoretical frameworks.
